title: Words like gems
hook: a stranger writes down Manikkavasagar's songs at Chidambaram, and they open with Shiva's name
carry: talk itself becomes japa: katha japah

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhairava is the flash that cuts the ego, the guardian at Shiva's door. Today, our last day in the Shiva Sutras, and Manikkavasagar again, near the end of his road.
screen: `THE FLASH THAT CUTS THE BOAST.` · `LAST DAY IN THE SHIVA SUTRAS.`

segments.voice: Years after the tree and the flood, Manikkavasagar has walked from temple to temple, singing. He comes at last to Chidambaram, the city of the dancing Shiva. There, tradition says, a stranger asks him to recite all his songs, and writes them down on palm leaves as he speaks. The next morning the bundle is found on the temple step, signed: written by the Lord of the sacred hall. The stranger was Shiva. And the songs open with five syllables: namachivaya.
screen: `A STRANGER WRITES THE SONGS DOWN.` → `SIGNED: THE LORD OF THE SACRED HALL.` → `IT OPENS: NAMACHIVAYA.`

segments.voice: The book is the Tiruvachakam, the sacred utterance, and Tamil Shaivas still sing it in homes and temples. Its first song opens namachivaya vazhga: long live namah shivaya, the five-syllable mantra. When the priests asked what the songs meant, tradition says Manikkavasagar pointed to the dancing Shiva, walked into the shrine, and was not seen again. The meaning was him. That mantra is the heart of a practice called japa: repeating a divine name, slowly, with attention, often on a string of a hundred and eight beads. Om namah shivaya, again and again, until the name is the groove the mind runs in. Now the Shiva Sutras, in the book's last section: katha japah. Katha is talk, conversation. For the awakened yogi, his conversation is japa. Commentators explain: japa keeps awareness of Shiva alive, again and again. For someone who rests in that awareness all the time, there's nothing left to switch on. The lines around it say the same of the body, keeping it going is the vow, and of giving: the gift is knowledge of the self. That's how a poet's spoken words could become scripture: they already carried the name. And it's why so many Hindus greet each other with a god's name, Ram Ram, Jai Shri Krishna, Har Har Mahadev, and murmur Shiva, Shiva while they cook. Not every word is holy yet. The practice is to say the name so often that, one day, the talk itself is japa.
screen: `THE TIRUVACHAKAM, SUNG TODAY.` · `JAPA: THE NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `KATHA JAPAH: TALK IS JAPA.` · `RAM RAM. HAR HAR MAHADEV.` · then, large: `TALK ITSELF BECOMES JAPA.`

segments.voice: Try japa the way it's done. Hold a mala if you have one, or count on the joints of your fingers, and say Om namah shivaya, softly or silently, eleven times, slowly enough to hear each syllable. Then let an ordinary thought come, and notice whether the name is still humming under it. If you don't pray, say the meaning instead: I bow to the auspicious one.
Katha japah. His conversation is japa: for one who rests in Shiva, ordinary talk already carries the name. That closes our time in the Shiva Sutras.
Your line: talk itself becomes japa, katha japah. Say the name until it hums under everything. Rest well.
